draft.title: The statistical inquiry process
card: Pose
Start with a clear question that data can answer, such as "How many hours do Year 9 students at our school sleep on school nights?"
Plan
Decide what data you need, who you will collect it from and how, such as a short survey with one question about hours of sleep.
Collect
Gather the data by following the plan and record it carefully, in a table or spreadsheet.
Analyse and report
Analyse the data with a graph and with measures such as the mean or median. Then report a conclusion that answers the original question.
draft.remember: A statistical inquiry runs from a question, to a plan, to data, to analysis, to a conclusion that answers the question.

a.q: Mia wants to find out how long students at her school spend travelling to school. She writes a survey form and decides which students to ask. Which step is she doing?
opts: Planning how to collect the data
Posing the question
Analysing the data
Reporting the conclusion
a.why: Writing the survey form and deciding who to ask is planning how to collect the data. Posing the question comes earlier, when Mia decides what she wants to find out.
a.clue: She has not collected any answers yet.

b.q: Tom asks "Do students at my school walk or ride to school?" He collects the answers and draws a graph. What should he do next to finish the inquiry?
opts: Write a conclusion that answers his question
Change the question to match the graph
Collect the data again with a new plan
Pose a second question about sport
b.why: The graph is the analysis. The inquiry ends with a conclusion that answers the original question, such as whether most students walk or ride. Collecting again or changing the question is not needed.
b.clue: The last step goes back to the question he first asked.

a.best: Planning how to collect the data

b.best: Write a conclusion that answers his question

problems.detail: The right option, 'Planning how to collect the data', is clearly the longest and the only one with extra detail. The others are two or three words each, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.
